Surah al-Saff (The Ranks)

It is also called Surat al-Hawariyyin (the Chapter of the Disciples) and Surat 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him. It is Medinan according to the majority of scholars, and this is related from Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, 'Ikrimah and Mujahid. Ibn Yasar said it is Meccan, and this is also related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. The preferred view is the first, and what supports it is what al-Hakim and others narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "We sat reading among the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and we discussed together, saying: 'If we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah, the Exalted, we would do them.' So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ and ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 1, 2]." 'Abdullah said: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it to us until he finished it." This hadith has also been narrated in a musalsal form (a chain in which a particular feature is repeated in each transmission), where the narrator says: "He recited it to us." It is a sound hadith according to the criteria of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and a great many others narrated it. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said: "It is the soundest musalsal hadith transmitted in this world, if anything comparable to it in its extraordinary closeness of chain has occurred among the musalsal narrations."

Likewise, what is related about the occasion of revelation from al-Dahhak, that it was the saying of some young Muslims: "We did such-and-such in the battle," when they had not done it. And what is related from Ibn Zayd, that it was the saying of the hypocrites to the believers: "We are with you and among you," then their actions appear to contradict that.

Its verses number fourteen, without disagreement. Its connection to what precedes it lies in its containing exhortation to jihad and encouragement toward it. Included in this is an emphasis on the prohibition against taking disbelievers as allies, which the preceding surah contained.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾. The discussion of it is like the discussion of its counterpart that has passed.

The address with the description of faith in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ is apparent according to all opinions except the last one concerning the occasion of revelation. Accordingly, it has been said that it is for mockery (al-tahakkum) of those hypocrites and of their faith.

"Li-ma" is composed of the prepositional lam and the interrogative ma, whose alif has been dropped, according to what the grammarians (al-nuhat) said, in order to distinguish between the declarative and the interrogative, and it was not reversed out of concern for the answer. It has also been said that it is because the two are used together very frequently, so it deserved lightening. Proving the aforementioned frequency is a difficult matter. It has also been said that it is because the two are closely joined in indicating the thing being asked about. This is explained by saying that when you say, "Why did you do it?" for example, the thing asked about is the cause (ʿillah) of the action. So it is like a compound of the cause and the action. The cause is indicated by the lam, and the action is indicated by ma, because it means "what thing." The whole compound conveys the meaning. When the particle that asks about the action is absent, the action alone is indicated, and that, as you see, is not the case. The meaning is: "For what thing do you say what you do not do of good and righteousness?!"

Moreover, the basis of the rebuke is in reality their not doing it. It was directed at their saying it only to draw attention to the multiplication of their disobedience, by making clear that what is denounced is not only abandoning the good that was promised, but also the promise itself, which they had considered to be good. Had it been said, "Why do you not do what you say?", it would have been understood from it that what is denounced is merely abandoning what was promised.

[p. 84]

*"It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do"* (61:3). This is an explanation (bayan) of the extreme ugliness of what they did. *Kabura* (it is great) is used in the pattern of *bi'sa* (an expression of blame), in which there is an ambiguous pronoun (*damir mubham*) explained by the indefinite noun that follows it, and *an taqulu* (that you say) is the thing being condemned (*al-makhsus bi-al-dhamm*). It is also permitted that the pronoun in *kabura* refers to the verbal noun understood from His words, *"Why do you say"* (61:2), meaning: it (i.e., the saying) is greatly hateful. Then *an taqulu* would be either an apposition (*badal*) to the implied pronoun or the predicate of an omitted subject. It has also been said that *kabura* is used here to express amazement (*ta'ajjub*) without its literal wording, as in the verse:

*"The neighbour of Jassas: we avenged Kulayb with her fang; her atonement has raised Kulayb's tooth."*

The purpose of amazement is to magnify the matter in the hearts of the listeners. The phrase *an taqulu* is attributed to *kabura*, and *maqtan* (hatred) is put in the accusative as a specification (*tafsir*), indicating that their saying "what they do not do" is pure hatred, without any admixture, because hatred has taken firm hold of it. The word *maqt* was chosen because it is the most intense and most forceful form of hatred. From it comes *nikah al-maqt* (the marriage of hatred), which is a man marrying his father's wife. He did not limit himself to making the hatred great, but made it the most intense and most vile. "With Allah" is even more emphatic than this, because when it is established that its hatefulness is great in the sight of Allah, before Whom every great thing is considered insignificant, then its greatness and severity are complete and doubts about it are removed.

Explaining *maqt* as I have mentioned has been adopted by more than one of the lexicographers (*ahl al-lughah*). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *maqt* is hatred because of a sin, a suspicion, or a baseness committed by the one who is hated. Al-Mubarrad said: "A man is *mamqut* and *maqit* when everyone hates him."

The verse has been used as evidence for the obligation of fulfilling a vow (*nadhr*). It is related from one of the early pious predecessors (*salaf*) that he was asked, "Narrate to us," and he remained silent. He was asked again, "Narrate to us," and he said: "And do you command me to say what I do not do? Then I would hasten to incur the hatred of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 61, verse 4:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks (saffan), as though they were a solid structure (bunyanun marsus)﴾ are an explanation of what is pleasing to Him, exalted is He, after the explanation of what is detested by Him, glorified is His majesty. The apparent meaning favours that what they (the Companions) said refers to a promise of fighting, rather than what is implied by what has been narrated from al-Dahhak or from Ibn Zayd regarding the occasion of revelation. It also implies that the basis of the rebuke is their failure to fulfil (their promise), not their promise. *Saffan* is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the place of an active participle (ism al-fa'il) or a passive participle (ism al-maf'ul). It is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal, the accusative of state) from the pronoun in *yuqatilun* (they fight), meaning: arranging themselves in rows, or being arranged in rows. *Ka'annahum* (as though they were) and what follows are a circumstantial clause from the concealed pronoun in the first circumstantial qualifier, meaning: likened in their close joining to a structure, and so on. This is what al-Zamakhshari intended by his saying: "They, i.e. *saffan* and *ka'annahum* and what follows, are two interlocking circumstantial qualifiers (hal mutadakhilan)." Ibn al-Munir's statement, that the meaning of interlocking is that the first circumstantial qualifier includes the second, since the state of being attached is the state of being compacted, differs from what is known of interlocking in the terminology of the grammarians. It has also been permitted that it be a second circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun.

Al-Hawfi said: it is in the position of a descriptive qualifier (na't) for *saffan*. That is, as you see, weak. Al-Farra' and Mundhir ibn Sa'id said that *marsus* means bound with lead, and it is intended to mean firm. Al-Mubarrad said: "I *rasastu* the building", meaning I joined its parts together and brought them close until it became like a single piece. From this comes *al-rasis*, which is the closing of the teeth. The apparent meaning is that the intention is to liken them, in the cohesion of some of them to others, to a solid structure, insofar as there is no gap between them and no fault. It has also been said that the intention is the evenness of their intentions in steadfastness, so that they are, in unity of word, like a solid structure. Most scholars hold the first view. In Ahkam al-Qur'an (Rulings of the Qur'an) it is said that this indicates the recommendation for holy warriors to stand for battle in rows, like the rows of prayer, and that it is recommended to close gaps and fill defects in the rows, to complete the first row before the next, and that levelling the rows means that none of them advances ahead of others in them. Ibn al-Firs said: some have used this as evidence that the fighting of infantry (rajjalah) is superior to the fighting of cavalry (furSan), because close formation is only possible for them. Then he said: "This is disputed." End of quotation. Then, fighting in this formation today is one of the foundations of the Muhammadan regular armies, may they ever remain victorious and supported by divine assistance. You know that means have the ruling of ends, so whatever leads to attaining this quality should not be neglected in its pursuit.

Zayd ibn Ali read *yuqatalun* (with the verb passive, and) with a fatha on the *ta'*, and it was read *yaqtulun* (they kill).

Page 85

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And when Musa said to his people: "O my people, why do you hurt me?"﴾ are a resumed sentence, establishing what precedes it regarding the heinousness of abandoning fighting.

﴿Idh﴾ is in the accusative as an object, governed by a hidden verb addressed to the master of those addressed, ﷺ, through a shift of address (*talwin*, a change in the mode of address). The meaning is: "Mention to these people who turn away from fighting the time when Moses, peace be upon him, said to the Children of Israel, when he urged them to fight the tyrants, saying: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, lest you turn about as losers﴾ [5:21]. They did not obey his command, and disobeyed him in the worst manner, when they said: ﴿O Moses, in it is a people of tyrants, and we will not enter it until they leave it. If they leave it, then we will enter﴾, up to His words, exalted is He: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting here﴾ [5:22–24]. They persisted in this with the utmost persistence, and they harmed him, peace be upon him, with the utmost harm. So he reproached them for this by saying: ﴿O my people, why do you harm me?﴾ through opposition and disobedience regarding what I commanded you, ﴿while you know that I am the Messenger of God to you﴾. This clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) that emphasizes the denial of harm and the negation of its cause. The "qad" is for affirming knowledge, not for diminishing or approximating it, since that does not suit the context. The form of the present tense indicates continuity: that is, while the state is that you know with certain knowledge, continuously, by witnessing what appeared at my hands of the dazzling miracles, the greatest of which is the destruction of your enemy and your deliverance from his dominion, that I am the Messenger of God to you, to guide you to the good of this world and the next. And among the requirements of your knowledge of this is that you should magnify me greatly and hasten to obey me. ﴿So when they deviated﴾, that is, they persisted in deviation and swerving from the truth which he, peace be upon him, brought, and continued in it, ﴿God caused their hearts to swerve﴾, that is, He turned them away from accepting the truth and from inclining toward what is right, because their choice was turned toward blindness and error. It is also said: that is, when they deviated in reality and in accordance with what they were upon in it, God, exalted is He, caused their hearts in external existence to swerve, since bringing into being follows the will, and the will follows knowledge, and knowledge follows what the thing is in reality. On both views there is no difficulty regarding the sequence. His words, exalted is He: ﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾ are a concluding parenthetical statement that confirms the content of what precedes concerning the causing to swerve, and indicates its cause; that is, He does not guide the people who depart from obedience, and who persist in error, to a guidance that leads to the desired goal. Otherwise, guidance to what leads to it is general for all. By "them" is meant either those specifically mentioned, and the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to censure them for defiance and to give defiance as the reason for the absence of guidance; or it is the category of defiant people, and they fall under their ruling by primary inclusion. It is said: whichever it is, it refers to what is in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So separate us from the defiant people﴾ [5:25], and His words, glory be to Him: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiant people﴾ [5:26].

Some have said: "idh" is an adverbial complement related to a verb supposed to be implied by what follows, such as "zaghu" (they swerved) and similar, and the sentence is conjoined to what precedes it as the conjunction of one narrative to another narrative.

Some scholars held that their harming him, peace be upon him, consisted of disparaging and belittling him personally, denying his signs, disobeying him in matters whose benefits return to them, their worship of the calf, their request to see God, exalted is He, openly, and denying the truth, which is the right of God, exalted is He, and his right, peace be upon him. What was mentioned first is what the eloquence of the noble composition requires and what sound taste approves.

﴿And when Jesus, son of Mary, said﴾: this may be governed by the same verb as the first "when" (idh), or it may be governed by an implied verb that is coordinated with the first one. ﴿O Children of Israel﴾: Perhaps he, peace be upon him, did not say "O my people" as Moses, peace be upon him, had said, but rather said "O Children of Israel" because he did not have the usual lineage among them, which is descent through the father. Alternatively, it is an indication that he acted according to the Torah and that he was like them in being of the people of Moses, peace be upon him, humbling himself, since he had no followers and no people. There is in this address a degree of appeal for compassion. It has been said that the appeal for compassion [is] by what has been mentioned,
[Page 86]
because of what it contains of honour, for they used to take pride in being related to Israel, peace be upon him.

﴿Indeed I am the Messenger of God to you, confirming what is before me of the Torah﴾: that is, sent to you by Him, exalted is He, while I am confirming. So the accusative of ﴿confirming﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier, "state" clause) relating to the pronoun concealed in ﴿Messenger﴾, which is its governing element. ﴿To you﴾ is connected to it, and it is a ẓarf laghw (a non-essential adverbial phrase) with no pronoun in it that would make it a possessor of a ḥāl. This ḥāl was mentioned because it is among the strongest motives for their confirming him, peace be upon him. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and giving good tidings of a Messenger who will come after me﴾ is coordinated with ﴿confirming﴾, and it is likewise a motive for confirming him, peace be upon him, insofar as the good tidings of this Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, occur in the Torah, as in His saying, exalted is He, in the twentieth chapter of the fifth book of it: "The LORD came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them; he shined forth from mount Paran, and he came with ten thousands of saints: from his right hand went a fiery law for them." And His saying, glorified is He, in the eleventh chapter of this book: "O Moses, I will raise them up a Prophet from among their brethren, like unto thee, and will put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak unto them all that I shall command him. And it shall come to pass, that whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him," and other passages. His words, peace be upon him, include that his religion is the confirmation of the Books of God, exalted is He, and of His Prophets, peace be upon them all, those who came before and those who came after. The clause ﴿who will come﴾ and so on is in the position of a qualifier to ﴿Messenger﴾, and likewise the clause of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿whose name is Aḥmad﴾. This noble name is a proper name for our Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, and on this is the verse of Ḥassān:

"God bless him, and those who encircle His Throne, and the good ones, upon the blessed Aḥmad."

It is authentically transmitted from the narrations of Mālik, al-Bukhārī, Muslim, al-Dārimī, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasā'ī, on the authority of Jubayr ibn Muṭ'im, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Indeed I have names: I am Muḥammad, I am Aḥmad, I am al-Ḥāshir (the Gatherer), at whose feet people will be gathered; I am al-Māḥī (the Eraser), by whom God erases disbelief; and I am al-'Āqib (the Last)." Al-'Āqib is the one after whom there is no Prophet. It is derived from the present tense of the first person, or it is an elative (af'al al-tafḍīl) from ḥāmidiyya (praising). It has been permitted that it be from maḥmūdiyya (being praised), on the basis that Aḥmad has been heard as an elative from it, as in "al-'awd aḥmad" (the old camel is more praiseworthy). Otherwise, the elative from the passive form is not analogical. It was read as ﴿min ba'dī﴾ with the vowel of the yā' being fatḥa. This good tiding from him, peace be upon him, concerning our Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, is among what the inimitable Qur'an has spoken of. Thus the denial of this by the Christians is a kind of raving. As for their saying: "If it had occurred, it would have been mentioned in the Gospel," the implication in this is disputed; and if it is granted, we say: it did occur in the Gospel, but its compilers, after Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised, omitted it, being content with what is in the Torah, the Psalms of David, peace be upon him, the books of Isaiah, Habakkuk, Jeremiah and others among the prophets, peace be upon them all.

It is possible that they did mention it, but the scholars of the Christians afterwards, out of love for their religion or for some other matter, dropped it; so it has been said. I say: The Gospels that are with the Christians are four:

The Gospel of Matthew, one of the twelve disciples. He compiled it in the Syriac language in the land of Palestine eight years after Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised. Its chapters number sixty-eight.

The Gospel of Mark, who was one of the seventy. He compiled it in the Frankish language in the city of Rome twelve years after the raising. Its chapters number forty-eight.

The Gospel of Luke, who was also one of the seventy. He compiled it in Alexandria in the Greek language. Its chapters number eighty-three.

The Gospel of John, the beloved of Christ. He compiled it in the city of Ephesus in the lands of Rome thirty years after the raising. Its chapters in the Coptic copies number thirty-three, and they differ. Within it is what fairness testifies is not the speech of God, mighty and majestic, nor the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, such as the story of his crucifixion, which they claim, and his burial, and his raising from the grave to heaven. So it is nothing
[Page 87]
but chronicles and biographies in which there is an account of some of the circumstances of Jesus, peace be upon him, his birth, his raising and the like, and some sayings of his, peace be upon him, in the manner of some books composed about some great and righteous people. So the omission of some circumstances does no harm. The words that the Mighty Qur'an has spoken, such as his speech in the cradle and his good tidings of our Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, are present; and in the Gospel of John is what is a good tiding of that for whoever is fair and follows the straight path and does not twist. In the fifteenth chapter of it, Jesus Christ said: "But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things." John also said: Christ said: "If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him. He that loveth me not keepth not my sayings: and the word which ye hear is not mine, but the Father's which sent me. ... But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you. Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you... If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father." And he also said: "It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you. And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin... I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now. Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come. He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you. All things that the Father hath are mine." And he also said: "If ye love me, keep my commandments. And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you. I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you." The word Paraclete (Farqalīṭ) is a term that announces praise. Its being intended as referring to our Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, is determined from his, peace be upon him, speech, which is beyond doubt for whoever God has lifted the veil of partisanship from his eyes. Some Christians have interpreted it as "the Praiser" (ḥammād), and some as "the one who praises" (ḥāmid), so its meaning contains an indication to his name, peace and blessings be upon him, Aḥmad. Some have interpreted it as "the Saviour", based on Jesus's saying, peace be upon him: "God will send another Saviour." In that case, what has been mentioned is not a good tiding of him, may God bless him and grant him peace, under the title of praise, but it is a good tiding of him, may God bless him and grant him peace, under the title of deliverance. Thus it may be used as evidence for the establishment of his prophethood, may God bless him and grant him peace, even if it is not used as evidence for what is in this verse here. Some have claimed that the Paraclete refers to fiery tongues that descended from heaven upon the disciples, and they performed signs and wonders. It is not hidden that describing him as "another" rules this out, if nothing preceded them other than him. ﴿So when he came to them﴾: that is, Jesus, peace be upon him, ﴿with the clear proofs﴾: that is, with the manifest miracles.

﴿They said﴾: this ﴿is clear sorcery﴾, pointing to what he, peace be upon him, had brought; so the masculine form is according to this consideration. It has been said: pointing to him, peace be upon him, and calling him a sorcerer is for exaggeration. This is supported by the reading of ʿAbdullāh, Ṭalḥa, al-A'mash and Ibn Thābit: "This is a sorcerer." That the subject of ﴿came to them﴾ is the pronoun of Jesus, peace be upon him, is the apparent meaning, because he is the one spoken of. It has also been said: it is the pronoun of Aḥmad, peace be upon him, when he finished speaking about Jesus and turned to report about Aḥmad, may God bless him and grant him peace; that is: "So when Aḥmad came to these disbelievers with the clear proofs, they said..." and so on.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah while he is being invited to Islam?﴾ That is, there are no people more unjust than one who is invited to Islam, which leads him to the happiness of both abodes, yet he puts in the place of acceptance the fabrication of lies against Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by denying His Messenger and calling His signs magic. The fabrication against Allah, exalted is He, encompasses denying what is established and affirming what is negated. That is, there is no one more unjust than that. What is meant is that he is more unjust than every wrongdoer. Talha read «يَدَّعِي» (yaddaʿī), the imperfect (muḍāriʿ, present tense) of ‑ادَّعى (idda'ā), in the active voice (mabnī lil-fāʿil), with its subject being the pronoun of Allah, exalted: "yadʿī" in the sense of "yadʿū" (invites). It is said: "daʿāhu" and "addaʿāhu," like "lamasahu" and "iltamasahu." It was also said that the subject is the pronoun of the fabricator. "Idda'ā" transitively takes its object directly, but since it is here taken to include the meaning of belonging and affiliation, it is followed by "ilā" (to). That is, "while he claims affiliation with Islam, asserting that he is a Muslim, and he is not that." And from him (is reported) «يُدَّعى» (yuddaʿā), also the imperfect of idda'ā, but in the passive voice (mabnī lil-maf'ūl), and its meaning is as previously mentioned. The verse concerns those among this community who denied, as indicated by what follows. If it concerns the Children of Israel, to whom Jesus, peace be upon him, came, then it lends support to the view that Islam is not restricted to the true religion brought by our Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ That is, He does not guide them to what their success lies in, due to their poor disposition and their failure to turn toward it.

[Page 88]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 61, verse 8:

﴿They want to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾ is an allegory for their state in their striving to nullify the truth, likened to the state of one who blows at the sun with his mouth to extinguish it, mocking and ridiculing them, just as people say: "He wants to put out the eye of the sun." Some eminent scholars held that what is meant by the light of Allah is His religion, the truth, as narrated from al-Suddi, by way of explicit metaphor (isti'arah tasrihiyyah). Likewise in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and Allah will perfect His light﴾, "mutimm" is an abstraction (tajrid), and in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with their mouths﴾ there is a double meaning (tawriyah). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd that they want to nullify the Qur'an and deny it by speech. Ibn Bahr said: they want to nullify the proofs of Allah, exalted is He, by their denial. Al-Dahhak said: they want the destruction of the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, through rumours. It was also said: they want to nullify the status of the Prophet (ﷺ) and to hide his manifestation through their speech and their lies. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that revelation was delayed for forty days, and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf said: "O assembly of Jews, rejoice! Allah has extinguished the light of Muhammad in what used to descend upon him, and He will not perfect his light." The Messenger (ﷺ) grieved, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿They want﴾ to its end.

Regarding ﴿They want to extinguish﴾ there are several views. First, that the lam is extra (za'idah) and the verb is in the subjunctive governed by an implied "an" after it; it was added to emphasize the meaning of desire, because the lam of causation carries the sense of intention and purpose, just as the lam is added in "la abaka lak" to emphasize the meaning of attribution. Second, that it is not an extra lam but a lam of causation, and the object of "yuridun" is omitted, meaning: they want the fabrication in order that they may extinguish. Third, that the verb "yuridun" itself is in the place of a verbal noun, is a subject (mubtada'), the lam is for causation, and the word governed by it is the predicate (khabar), meaning: their desire is for the extinguishing; the sentence is, in one respect, like "tasma' bil-mu'idiyyi khayrun min an tarah" (you hear of al-Mu'idi is better than that you see him). Fourth, that the lam is verbal-noun-forming (masdariyyah), with the meaning of "an" without any implied element, and the verbal noun is the direct object; this is common after the verbs of desire and command. Fifth, that ﴿yuridun﴾ is treated as if intransitive, being interpreted as "they cause desire to occur," and it was said: in this there is exaggeration, in making every desire they have directed toward extinguishing; and there is discussion of this in the commentary on al-Mughni and elsewhere.

The two Iraqi readers (al-'Arabiyyan), Nafi', Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, Talhah, al-A'raj and Ibn Muhaysin read "mutimmu" with tanwin and "nurahu" in the accusative, as the object of "mutimmun." ﴿And though the disbelievers dislike it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in "mutimmu," and in it is an indication that He, mighty and majestic is He, will perfect it, humiliating them.

He it is who sent His Messenger, Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿with guidance﴾, meaning with the Qur'an, or with the miracle, making that itself guidance as an intensification; ﴿and the religion of truth﴾, and the upright creed (al-millah al-hanifiyyah); ﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾, that He may exalt it above all religions opposed to it. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has indeed fulfilled His promise, for He made it such that no religion remains except that it is overcome and subdued by the religion of Islam.

It is narrated from Mujahid: "When 'Isa (peace be upon him) descends, there will be nothing on earth but the religion of Islam." What is reported, that there will come upon people a time in which nothing of Islam remains except its name, does not conflict with this, since the verse does not indicate permanence. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "prevailing" is exaltation in terms of the clarity of the proofs and the brightness of the evidences, and that is a matter that continues forever. ﴿And even though the polytheists dislike it﴾

that is because of what it contains of pure monotheism and the nullification of polytheism. It was also read: "He it is who sent His Prophet (nabiyyahu)."

﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a commerce﴾ of great significance ﴿that will save you from a painful punishment﴾ on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'raj, and Ibn Amir recited «تُنَجِّيكم» with tashdid (the doubling of the letter jim, marked by a shaddah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 61, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives﴾ is an explanatory resumption (istiʾnaf bayani), as if it were said: "What is this commerce? Point us to it." So it is said: ﴿You believe﴾, and so on. The present-tense verb in both places, as al-Mubarrad and a group [of grammarians] said, is a report with the meaning of a command, i.e. "Believe and strive." This is supported by the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) which is likewise. The expression of it in this form is to signal that compliance is obligatory, as if faith and jihad had already taken place, so He informed of their occurrence. If the address is to the sincere believers, then the meaning is "persist and continue in faith," or "combine faith and jihad," i.e. combine the perfecting of the self with the perfecting of others. If the address is to those who are outwardly believers, then the meaning is "make your faith sincere." In either case there is no difficulty in the command.

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿You believe﴾, and so on, is an appositive (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿a commerce﴾. It was objected that this is not conceivable except on the assumption that the original was "an tuʾminu" (that you believe), so that it could be parsed as a verbal noun, then "an" was deleted and the verb became marfuʿ (nominative), as in his saying: "Alā ayyuhadha al-zajiri ahḍura al-waghā" (meaning: "an aḥḍura", that I attend the battle), and when "an" was deleted the verb became marfuʿ, which is rare.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: ﴿You believe﴾ is a verb in the nominative, by the assumption "that you believe" (annahu tuʾminuna). In this there is deletion of the subject and of "an" with its noun while its predicate is retained, and that, according to Abu Hayyan, is not permitted.

Zayd ibn ʿAli read "tuʾminu" and "tujahidu" (without the nun), by deleting the nun of the nominative in both, assuming an implied imperative lam: "li-tuʾminu wa-tujahidu," i.e. "so that you believe and strive," or "wa-li-tujahidu," as in his saying:

"I said to a doorkeeper at its gate: Permit us, for I am among its close relatives."

And likewise his saying:

"Muhammad, let yourself be ransomed by every soul, if you fear any misfortune that befalls."

It is also permitted to take it as a resumption (istiʾnaf), and the nun was deleted for lightness, as in the reading "sahiranı yaẓẓahara" and his saying:

"Pluck as much as you wish to pluck; the trap has been raised, so what will you beware of?"

And likewise his saying:

"I spend the night keeping vigil while you sleep and rub your face with ambergris and fragrant musk."

You know that this deletion is anomalous.

﴿That﴾, i.e. what has been mentioned of faith and jihad, ﴿is better for you﴾ absolutely, or [better] than your wealth and your lives, ﴿if you know﴾, i.e. if you are among the people of knowledge, for the ignorant are not credited with their deeds so as to be described as good. It was also said: i.e. if you know that it is better for you, it will be better for you then, because when you know that and believe it, you will love faith and jihad more than you love your wealth and your lives, so you will be sincere and succeed.

﴿يَغْفِرْ لَكم ذُنُوبَكُمْ﴾ is a response (jawab) to an imperative that is implied by a declarative form, as in their saying: "May a man who fears God Most High and does good be rewarded for it." Or it is a response to a conditional, or to an interrogative that the context implies, and the sense is: "If you believe and strive, He will forgive you." Or: "Would you accept that I guide you?" Or: "Would you trade in faith and jihad?" Then: "He will forgive you." Al-Farra' said: it is a response to the interrogative mentioned, i.e., "Shall I guide you?" This was objected to on the ground that mere guidance does not necessitate forgiveness. The reply is that it is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Tell My servants who believe to establish the prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31]. Some have said about this verse that since the command was addressed to a firm believer, it was the likely cause of compliance, so it was treated as though its occurrence were certain. Here too, it is said: since guidance is the likely cause of that, it takes the place of what is certain. This is supported by ﴿if you know﴾, because whoever has intellect, when his master points him to what is good for him, does not leave it. As for the claim that the phrase "your sins" is an honorific idafah (possessive construction), and that what is here is a rebuke, it has been said that this is not evident, so reflect. The fair assessment is that al-Farra's explanation is not free from remoteness.

Page 90

As for what has been said, that the sentence is a new independent clause explaining that this is good for them, and that "yaghfir" is in the nominative case with its final letter made quiescent, as the final letter of "ashrab" was made quiescent in his saying:

*So today I drink, not bearing a sin from God,*
*nor as one who sneaks in uninvited.*

this is worthless, for they have stated that this is a case of necessity (ḍarūrah, poetic license). ﴿And He will admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings﴾, that is, pure, wholesome and delightful. This indicates their goodness in themselves. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in gardens of perpetual residence﴾ indicates their goodness with regard to their place. ﴿That﴾, that is, what has been mentioned of forgiveness and what has been joined to it, ﴿is the great triumph﴾, beyond which there is no triumph.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 61, verse 13:

﴿Wa-ukhrā﴾ means: and for you, in addition to the blessings mentioned, there is another blessing. "Ukhrā" is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), but in reality it is a *sifah* (qualifier) of an omitted *mubtada'*, which was replaced by it after the omission. The *khabar* (predicate) is omitted. This is the view of al-Farra'. The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿tuhibbūnahā﴾ ("which you love"), are in the position of a qualifier. His words, glorified is He, ﴿naṣrun mina Llāhi wa-fatḥun qarīb﴾ ("help from Allah and a near victory"), i.e. imminent, are a *badal* (substitution) or an *'atf bayān* (explanatory apposition). The nominal sentence consisting of the *mubtada'* and its *khabar* is said to be a *ḥāliyyah* (circumstantial clause). In al-Kashf, it is said that it is coordinated (*'atf*) with the response to the imperative, namely "yughfir" (He will forgive), in meaning, just as you say: "Strive, you will be rewarded, and you will have the spoils." The phrase ﴿tuhibbūnahā﴾ is an expression addressed to them, and likewise the choice of the nominal form over the verbal form and its coordination with it, as if this [blessing] is in their view more firmly established and more attainable, and their souls are more at rest in attaining it and in success.

It is said: "Ukhrā" is a *mubtada'* whose *khabar* is "naṣr" (help). Some people said: it is in the position of an accusative (*naṣb*) by an implied verb, i.e. "and He will give you another," and this has been treated as an instance of the line:

*"I fed her chaff and cold water."*

Some of them estimated "tuḥibbūna ukhrā" (you love another), taking it to be of the *ishtighāl* construction (verb preoccupied with a pronoun referring to the subject). According to both estimates, "naṣrun" is the *khabar* of an omitted *mubtada'*, i.e. "that is" or "it is naṣr," or it is a *mubtada'* whose *khabar* is omitted, i.e. "help and a near victory are with Him." Al-Akhfash said: it is in the position of a genitive (*jarr*) by coordination with "tijārah" (trade), and this, as you see, is [weak].

Ibn Abi 'Abla read "naṣran wa-fatḥan qarīban" with the accusative, by an implied "a'nī" (I mean), or as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), i.e. "you will be helped with help, and a victory will be granted to you," or as a substitution for "ukhrā" if it is read in the accusative. "Wa-bashshiri al-mu'minīn" (and give good news to the believers) is coordinated with an implied "qul" (say) before His words: ﴿yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū﴾ (O you who believe). It is also said that it is coordinated with an implied "abshir" (give good news), and the estimate is: "So give good news, O Muhammad, and give good news."

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is coordinated with "tu'minūn" (you believe), because it has the meaning of a command, as if it were said: "Believe and strive, Allah will reward you and help you, and give good news, O Messenger of Allah, to the believers of this." Al-Ighdah (Ibn al-Hajib's commentary?) [no: this is the author's remark] objected to this, saying that there is a problem with it, because the addressees of "tu'minūn" are the believers, whereas in "bashshir" the one addressed is the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Furthermore, His words "tu'minūn" are an explanation of what precedes it by way of resumption (*isti'nāf*), so how can "bashshiri al-mu'minīn" be coordinated with it? It was answered with a summary to the effect that His words, glorified is He, ﴿yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū﴾ are addressed to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his community, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence. When it is interpreted as "Believe and give good news," it indicates his, upon him be blessing and peace, profitable trade and their righteous trade. He placed "āmanū" first because it is the opening of everything. Then, even if this is accepted, there is no obstacle to coordination with the answer to the questioner by something that is not an answer if it suits him, so that it becomes an answer to the question and an addition. How much more so when it is included within it! As if they said: "Guide us, O our Lord," and it was said: "Believe, and it will be yours, such-and-such, and give them good news, O Muhammad, of its being established for them." In this there is, as is not hidden, the nobility of its placement from the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun and the variation of address. The author of al-Kashf preferred it, saying: this aspect is one of the aspects of coordination with "qul" (say). Coordination with "fa-abshir" (so give good news) was also considered valid, since the two lack the benefits mentioned, meaning what the answer includes.

[Page 91]

That is, to support His religion, may He be glorified, and to aid His Messenger, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him. Al-A'raj, 'Isa, Abu 'Amr, and the two Haramis (the Meccan and Medinan readers) read *anṣāran lillāh* with *tanwīn* (nunation, the final "-n" sound on the noun). The *tanwīn* here indicates partitive meaning (*li-l-tab'īḍ*), so the sense is: "be some of His helpers, may He be exalted and glorified."

Ibn Mas'ud read, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, *kūnū antum anṣāra llāh* ("be you the helpers of God"). According to Mu'ahhah al-Ahwazi and al-Kawashi, the reading is *antum* without *kūnū*. (The verse continues:) ﴿As Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples: "Who will be my helpers in God's cause?"﴾, meaning: "Who among you will be my soldier, turning toward supporting God, the Exalted?" This is so that it corresponds with His words, may He be glorified: ﴿The disciples said: "We are God's helpers."﴾ It has also been said that *ilā* here means *ma'a* (with), and the sense is "Who will be my helpers with God?" and "We are God's helpers," taking the implied meaning "We are the helpers of the Prophet of God," thus achieving correspondence. The first view is preferable. The *iḍāfa* (genitive construction) in ﴿my helpers﴾ is the construction of one of two partners to the other, because when they both shared in supporting God, the Exalted, there was a connection between them that justifies attributing one to the other. The *iḍāfa* in ﴿helpers of God﴾ is the construction of the agent to the object. The comparison is in terms of meaning, since the intended sense is: "Say to them that, as Jesus said." Abu Hayyan said: "It means: 'We have told you as Jesus said.'"

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It means: 'Be helpers of God as the disciples were helpers of Jesus when he said to them: "Who will be my helpers in God's cause?"'" Its essence, as has been said, is that *mā* is a verbal-masdar particle (*mā maṣdariyya*), and together with its clause it forms an adverbial of time, meaning: "Be helpers of God at the time of my saying to you, like the disciples' being His helpers at the time of Jesus' saying." Then it was said: "Be His helpers in the manner of the time when Jesus spoke these words." The narrative of his asking about a helper and their reply has been introduced, so it is like *ka-l-yawm* in their saying *ka-l-yawm rajul* ("like today, a man"), meaning "like a man I saw today," where the noun and its adjective are omitted and the adverb of time is used instead, because it indicates the verb that indicates the noun it modifies. This is one of their broad uses of adverbs of time. The verse has also been classed as *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which parallel elements are omitted from each part, each part supplying what is missing in the other). The underlying sense is: "Be helpers of God at the time when the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to you: 'Who will be my helpers in God's cause?', as the disciples were helpers of God at the time when Jesus, peace be upon him, said to them: 'Who will be my helpers in God's cause?'" So from each of the two parts there is omitted what the mentioned part in the other indicates. This is not without elegance.

The *ḥawāriyyūn* (disciples) were his chosen companions, peace be upon him. The shift from the pronoun for them to the noun is to emphasize their status. They were the first to believe in him, and they were twelve men. According to al-Bahr, Jesus, peace be upon him, dispersed them throughout the lands: some he sent to Rome, some to Babylon, some to Africa, some to Ephesus, some to Jerusalem, some to the Hijaz, and some to the land of the Berbers and its surroundings. The identification of who was sent to each place is included in this, but I am not confident in its accuracy or in the vocalization of their names. Al-Suyuti also mentioned them in *al-Itqan*, so the verification of this should be sought in its proper sources.

The derivation of *ḥawāriyyīn* is from *ḥawar*, which means whiteness. They were named thus because they were launderers (*qaṣṣārīn*). It has also been said that it is because of their wearing white, or because of the purity of their outward and inward states. Some claim that what has been said about them being launderers is an indication that they purified people's souls by conveying religion and knowledge, and what has been said about them being fishermen is an indication that they caught people's souls out of confusion and led them to the truth.

It has been said that the *ḥawāriyyūn* are the fighters for God's cause (*mujāhidūn*). In a hadith: "Every prophet has a disciple (*ḥawārī*), and my disciple is al-Zubayr." It has been interpreted as meaning the intimate and special among the companions and the helpers. Al-Azhari said: "It refers to one who is sincere and free of every defect." From Qatada, the term *ḥawārī* is applied to others as well, may God be pleased with them. He said: "All the disciples were from Quraysh: Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali, Hamza, Ja'far, Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 'Uthman ibn Maz'un, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah, and al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, may God be pleased with them all."

[Page 92]

﴿So a group of the Children of Israel believed﴾, that is, in Jesus, peace be upon him. ﴿And another group disbelieved.﴾ ﴿So We supported those who believed against their enemy﴾, and they were those who disbelieved, ﴿and they became victorious﴾, meaning they became dominant. Zayd ibn 'Ali and Qatada said: "By argument and proof." It has been said that when Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised to heaven, a group of his people said: "He is God, may He be exalted," and another group said: "He is the son of God, may God be exalted far above that, a great exaltation," and God, may He be glorified, raised him to Himself. Another group said: "He is the servant of God and His messenger." They fought, and the two disbelieving groups prevailed over the believing group until the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was sent, and the believing group prevailed over the two disbelieving groups. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said that the believers and the disbelievers fought after his raising, peace be upon him, and the believers prevailed over the disbelievers by the sword. It is well known that fighting was not part of his law, peace be upon him. It has also been said that the meaning is: ﴿So a group of the Children of Israel believed﴾ in Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, and another group disbelieved in him, may God bless him and grant him peace. So We supported the believers against the disbelievers, and they became dominant. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. And God knows best.
